title: CBT interventions and techniques
description: Catalog of CBT interventions and techniques a therapist delivers, grouped cognitive, behavioral, exposure, emotion and compassion, relational and session process, and condition-specific. Used to code the intervention or treatment-target slots of a formulation and treatment plan. Client coping actions belong in cs; therapist competencies in ts; instruments in ms.
sources: Craske-etal-2014 § Strategies for optimizing inhibitory learning

concepts.label: Identifying automatic thoughts
concepts.definition: Helping the client notice and record the thoughts and images present when their emotion shifts, then select the hot thought to work on.
concepts.client_wording: Noticing what goes through your mind when your mood suddenly changes.
concepts.example: "What was going through your mind just then, when you went quiet?"

concepts.label: Cognitive restructuring
concepts.definition: Collaboratively examining an automatic thought's accuracy and usefulness through guided questions, then building a more balanced, believable alternative response.
concepts.client_wording: Checking whether a thought fits the facts and finding a fairer way to see things.
concepts.example: "What is the evidence for this thought? Is there another way of looking at it?"
sources: Beck-2021 § Ch. 15 Responding to Automatic Thoughts

concepts.label: Thought record
concepts.definition: Structured worksheet linking situation, moods, automatic thoughts, evidence for and against the hot thought, and a balanced alternative, with ratings before and after.
concepts.client_wording: A worksheet for catching an upsetting thought, weighing it up and finding a more balanced view.
concepts.example: After a friend cancels plans, the client completes a seven-column record and sadness falls from 80 to 40.
sources: Beck-2021 § Ch. 15 Responding to Automatic Thoughts

concepts.label: Decatastrophizing
alt_labels: worst, best and most likely outcome
concepts.definition: Examining a feared outcome by estimating its realistic likelihood, the worst, best and most likely outcomes, and how the client would cope.
concepts.client_wording: Thinking through what would really happen if the worst came true, and how you would cope.
concepts.example: "If you did fail the exam, what would you do next, and how would you get through it?"
sources: Leahy-2017 § Ch. 9 Putting Things in Perspective

concepts.label: Double-standard technique
alt_labels: what would you tell a friend
concepts.definition: Asking how the client would view or advise a friend with the same thought or situation, then applying that kinder standard to themselves.
concepts.client_wording: Treating yourself the way you would treat a good friend in the same spot.
concepts.example: "If your best friend made this mistake, would you tell her she is useless?"

concepts.label: Responsibility pie chart
concepts.definition: Dividing a pie chart among all contributing factors to an event, rating own share last, to correct inflated personal responsibility or blame.
concepts.client_wording: Drawing a pie to see how much of what happened was really down to you.
concepts.example: The client allots slices to weather, the other driver and roadworks; their own share drops from 100% to 20%.
sources: Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 15 Understanding Your Anger, Guilt, and Shame

concepts.label: Advantages-disadvantages analysis
concepts.definition: Listing and weighing the short- and long-term advantages and disadvantages of holding a belief, keeping a rule, or making a change.
concepts.client_wording: Weighing up the pros and cons of a belief, a rule you live by, or a habit.
concepts.example: Pros and cons of the rule "I must never say no to anyone".

concepts.label: Identifying cognitive distortions
concepts.definition: Teaching the client to recognize recurring biased thinking patterns, such as catastrophizing or mind reading, and label them in their own thoughts.
concepts.client_wording: Learning to spot common thinking traps so you can step back from them.
concepts.example: "That sounds like mind reading again: you are guessing what he thinks."
sources: Burns-1980 § Ch. 3 You Feel the Way You Think
Leahy-2017 § Ch. 12 Examining and Challenging Cognitive Distortions

concepts.label: Downward arrow
concepts.definition: Repeatedly asking what a thought would mean if it were true, to move from an automatic thought to underlying assumptions and core beliefs.
concepts.client_wording: Asking "and if that were true, what would it mean?" to find the deeper worry.
concepts.example: "I'll make a mistake" leads to "They'll see I'm incompetent" leads to "I'm a failure."

concepts.label: Modifying rules and assumptions
concepts.definition: Identifying conditional assumptions and rigid rules, examining their costs and origins, testing them with behavioral experiments, and building more flexible versions.
concepts.client_wording: Finding the unwritten rules you live by and making them more flexible and helpful.
concepts.example: "If I'm not perfect, I'll be rejected" is tested and revised to "Good enough is usually accepted."
sources: Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 11 Underlying Assumptions and Behavioral Experiments

concepts.label: Core belief work
concepts.definition: Identifying an unhelpful core belief, then constructing and strengthening an alternative belief over time with evidence logs, historical review, continua and experiential methods.
concepts.client_wording: Gradually building a kinder, more accurate view of yourself, other people or the world.
concepts.example: Over several months the client strengthens "I am acceptable as I am" alongside the old belief "I am defective."

concepts.label: Positive data log
concepts.definition: Daily written record of everyday experiences consistent with a new, more adaptive core belief, countering biased attention to belief-confirming information.
concepts.client_wording: Writing down, each day, small things that fit a new, more helpful view of yourself.
concepts.example: New belief "I am likeable": "Neighbor stopped to chat; colleague thanked me for my help."
sources: Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 12 New Core Beliefs, Gratitude, and Acts of Kindness

concepts.label: Continuum technique
concepts.definition: Rating self or others on a 0 to 100 scale with explicitly defined anchors, to replace all-or-nothing judgments with graded ones.
concepts.client_wording: Placing yourself on a scale instead of seeing yourself as all good or all bad.
concepts.example: The client first rates self 0 on "lovable"; after defining the anchors, places self at 65.

concepts.label: Imagery rescripting
concepts.definition: Recalling a distressing memory or intrusive image in imagination, then changing its course to meet unmet needs and update its meaning.
concepts.client_wording: Revisiting a painful memory in your mind's eye and changing how it plays out.
concepts.example: The client imagines their adult self stepping into a childhood scene to protect and comfort the younger self.

concepts.label: Worry postponement
concepts.definition: Noticing worry, deferring it to a set daily worry period, then using that period briefly, to weaken worry and test beliefs about uncontrollability.
concepts.client_wording: Putting worries aside until a set worry time later in the day.
concepts.example: The client notes worries on a card and saves them for 15 minutes at 6 pm; many no longer seem urgent.

concepts.label: Rumination-focused techniques
concepts.definition: Functional analysis of rumination, then shifting from abstract, evaluative thinking to concrete, specific processing, absorption in experience, and self-compassion.
concepts.client_wording: Noticing when you are going round in circles and switching to more specific, useful thinking.
concepts.example: "How did this happen, and what is one step I can take?" replaces "Why does this always happen to me?"
sources: Watkins-2016 § Shifting Processing Style: Becoming Concrete and Specific

concepts.label: Detached mindfulness
concepts.definition: Metacognitive therapy stance of noticing thoughts as passing mental events without engaging, analyzing, suppressing or acting on them.
concepts.client_wording: Noticing a thought and letting it be, without arguing with it or following it.
concepts.example: The client notices "What if I get ill?" and watches it like a cloud passing, without starting to worry.

concepts.label: Behavioral activation
concepts.definition: Structured approach that increases contact with rewarding, valued activity and targets avoidance, using activity monitoring, scheduling and functional analysis of behavior.
concepts.client_wording: Gradually doing more of what matters to you, even before you feel like it.
concepts.example: A withdrawn client schedules a short walk and a call to a friend on three days and rates mood afterward.

concepts.label: Activity monitoring
concepts.definition: Hour-by-hour record of what the client does, with ratings of mood, mastery and pleasure, to reveal links between activity and mood.
concepts.client_wording: Keeping a simple diary of what you do each hour and how you feel.
concepts.example: The diary shows mood is lowest on afternoons spent in bed and higher after seeing people.

concepts.label: Activity scheduling
concepts.definition: Planning specific valued, pleasurable or mastery activities at set times in advance, then reviewing what happened and how mood changed.
concepts.client_wording: Planning specific activities into your week, then checking how they went.
concepts.example: "Tuesday 10 am: 20-minute walk to the park; Thursday 7 pm: call my sister."

concepts.label: Graded task assignment
concepts.definition: Breaking an overwhelming task or goal into small, sequential steps that are attempted in order, starting with one the client is likely to complete.
concepts.client_wording: Breaking a big task into small steps and taking them one at a time.
concepts.example: "Sort the mail" becomes: open envelopes for 10 minutes, then pay the one urgent bill.

concepts.label: Behavioral experiment
concepts.definition: Planned activity that tests a specific prediction or belief through direct experience, with a written prediction, belief rating, outcome and conclusion.
concepts.client_wording: A planned real-life test of a worrying prediction, to see what actually happens.
concepts.example: Prediction "If I speak up in the meeting, people will laugh" (belief 80%); outcome: one person agreed.
sources: Bennett-Levy-etal-2004 § Ch. 1 Behavioural experiments: historical and conceptual underpinnings
Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 11 Underlying Assumptions and Behavioral Experiments

concepts.label: Problem-solving therapy
concepts.definition: Structured steps: define the problem, generate options, weigh pros and cons, choose, plan, act and review, alongside work on negative problem orientation.
concepts.client_wording: A step-by-step way to tackle a real problem: list options, pick one, try it, review.
concepts.example: The client lists five ways to handle rent arrears, chooses to call the landlord, and plans what to say.

concepts.label: Relaxation training
concepts.definition: Teaching skills such as progressive muscle relaxation, slow breathing or applied (cue-controlled) relaxation to lower physiological arousal and use as a coping skill.
concepts.client_wording: Learning ways to relax your muscles and breathing so your body can settle.
concepts.example: After practicing daily, the client uses cue-controlled relaxation at the first sign of tension at work.

concepts.label: Safety behavior reduction
concepts.definition: Identifying safety behaviors and reassurance seeking, then dropping or fading them, often within experiments, so feared outcomes can be disconfirmed.
concepts.client_wording: Gradually letting go of the things you do to feel safe, to learn you are OK without them.
concepts.example: The client gives a short talk without gripping notes or avoiding eye contact and finds it goes better.

concepts.label: Self-monitoring
concepts.definition: Client records a target behavior, symptom, thought or urge as it happens, with context, to establish a baseline, reveal patterns and track change.
concepts.client_wording: Keeping track of something as it happens, so we can spot patterns together.
concepts.example: The client logs each binge urge with time, place, mood and what happened next.

concepts.label: Interpersonal effectiveness and assertiveness training
concepts.definition: Teaching and rehearsing clear, respectful requests, refusals and opinions through instruction, modeling, role play and feedback, balancing goals, relationship and self-respect.
concepts.client_wording: Practicing asking for what you need or saying no, clearly and respectfully.
concepts.example: The client role-plays asking a manager for a deadline extension, then tries it at work.

concepts.label: Behavior chain analysis
alt_labels: functional analysis of a problem behavior
concepts.definition: Detailed step-by-step review of vulnerabilities, prompting event, links and consequences of a specific problem behavior, to identify points where change is possible.
concepts.client_wording: Going through, step by step, what led up to a problem behavior and what followed.
concepts.example: Poor sleep, then an argument, then the thought "I can't stand this", then self-harm urge, then relief.
sources: Linehan-2025 § Chain analysis of problem behavior

concepts.label: Exposure
concepts.definition: Repeated, planned contact with feared but objectively safe stimuli, without avoidance or safety behaviors, so new non-threat learning can occur.
concepts.client_wording: Facing what you fear, step by step and on purpose, so you learn it is safer than it feels.
concepts.example: A client afraid of dogs moves from watching videos to standing near a calm dog on a leash.

concepts.label: Exposure hierarchy
concepts.definition: Collaboratively listed feared situations with predicted distress ratings, used to plan the order, variety and progression of exposure tasks.
concepts.client_wording: A ladder of feared situations, from easier to harder, that we use to plan practice.
concepts.example: Rungs run from riding one bus stop with a friend (SUDS 30) to a rush-hour train alone (SUDS 90).

concepts.label: In vivo exposure
concepts.definition: Exposure to real feared or avoided situations, objects or activities, in session or in daily life.
concepts.client_wording: Practicing facing feared situations in real life.
concepts.example: The client with agoraphobia walks alone to the supermarket and stays until the planned task is done.

concepts.label: Imaginal exposure
concepts.definition: Repeatedly and vividly imagining or narrating a feared scenario or traumatic memory, usually in the present tense, without avoidance, to process it.
concepts.client_wording: Picturing or describing a feared scene or memory in detail until it becomes less overwhelming.
concepts.example: A client with obsessions writes and rereads a script of the feared outcome until its impact falls.

concepts.label: Interoceptive exposure
concepts.definition: Deliberately inducing feared bodily sensations, such as dizziness, breathlessness or a racing heart, through exercises, so the client learns they are safe.
concepts.client_wording: Bringing on scary body feelings on purpose, to learn they are uncomfortable but not dangerous.
concepts.example: The client spins in a chair for 60 seconds to bring on dizziness and rates fear before and after.

concepts.label: Inhibitory learning strategies
concepts.definition: Designing exposure to maximize violation of specific feared predictions, vary stimuli and contexts, combine cues, remove safety signals and label affect.
concepts.client_wording: Setting up practice to test exactly what you fear will happen, in many different situations.
concepts.example: "What do you predict will happen, and what would tell us the prediction was wrong?"
sources: Craske-etal-2014 § Strategies for optimizing inhibitory learning

concepts.label: Emotion awareness training
concepts.definition: Teaching the client to identify, label and rate emotions and their components (thoughts, sensations, urges) with present-focused, nonjudgmental awareness.
concepts.client_wording: Learning to notice, name and rate what you are feeling.
concepts.example: The client distinguishes "anxious 70" from "ashamed 50" in the same situation.
sources: Greenberger-Padesky-2016 § Ch. 4 Identifying and Rating Moods

concepts.label: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT)
concepts.definition: Eight-week group program of guided mindfulness practices with cognitive elements, helping people disengage from ruminative patterns to prevent depressive relapse.
concepts.client_wording: A course of mindfulness practice that helps you step out of patterns that bring depression back.
concepts.example: A client in remission uses the three-minute breathing space when low mood begins to pull into rumination.

concepts.label: Compassionate mind training
concepts.definition: Compassion-focused exercises, such as soothing rhythm breathing, compassionate self imagery and compassionate letters, building capacity to meet distress and self-criticism with warmth.
concepts.client_wording: Practicing a warm, supportive inner voice to use when you are struggling or self-critical.
concepts.example: The client writes a letter to themselves about a setback from the viewpoint of a wise, kind friend.

concepts.label: Distress tolerance skills
concepts.definition: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) crisis survival skills, such as TIPP, distraction, self-soothing and pros and cons, for getting through intense urges without worsening things.
concepts.client_wording: Skills to get through a crisis moment without making it worse.
concepts.example: With a strong urge to self-harm, the client uses cold water on the face and paced breathing, then calls a friend.

concepts.label: Emotion regulation skills training
concepts.definition: DBT skills for understanding emotions, checking the facts, opposite action, problem solving, and reducing vulnerability through sleep, eating, exercise and positive events.
concepts.client_wording: Learning skills to understand your emotions and change the ones that are not helping you.
concepts.example: Shame urges hiding; the client checks the facts, then acts opposite by joining the conversation.

concepts.label: Socialization to CBT
concepts.definition: Orienting the client to the cognitive model, the structured collaborative format, homework and their active role, using examples from their own life.
concepts.client_wording: Explaining how CBT works and what we will do together, using your own examples.
concepts.example: "When she didn't reply, you thought 'she's angry with me' and felt anxious. Can you see the link?"
sources: Beck-2021 § Ch. 6 The First Therapy Session

concepts.label: Sharing the formulation
concepts.definition: Co-constructing and presenting the case formulation with the client, inviting correction, to explain the problem and guide choice of interventions.
concepts.client_wording: Building a picture together of what keeps the problem going, so we can choose what to change.
concepts.example: Therapist and client draw the vicious cycle on paper and the client adds a missing safety behavior.

concepts.label: Action plan (homework)
concepts.definition: Collaboratively designed between-session task that applies session learning, with a clear rationale, specific plan, anticipated obstacles and a review next session.
concepts.client_wording: A small task to try between sessions, so the changes carry into your week.
concepts.example: "Complete one thought record when you feel a strong mood shift; we'll review it next week."

concepts.label: Routine outcome monitoring with feedback
concepts.definition: Regularly administering standardized measures and reviewing scores and trends with the client to detect non-response and guide treatment decisions.
concepts.client_wording: Filling in short questionnaires regularly and looking at the results together to check progress.
concepts.example: PHQ-9 scores are graphed weekly; a plateau at session 6 prompts a review of the plan.

concepts.label: Motivational interviewing
concepts.definition: Collaborative, person-centered method for strengthening a person's own motivation and commitment to change by evoking and exploring their reasons.
concepts.client_wording: Talking through your own reasons for and against change, at your own pace.
concepts.example: "On a scale of 0 to 10, how important is cutting down? Why a 6 and not a 3?"
sources: Miller-Rollnick-2023 § Engaging, focusing, evoking and planning

concepts.label: Relapse prevention blueprint
concepts.definition: End-of-treatment written plan summarizing what was learned, helpful skills, early warning signs, likely high-risk situations, and steps to take after setbacks.
concepts.client_wording: A written plan to keep your progress going and handle setbacks after therapy ends.
concepts.example: The blueprint lists warning signs (skipping meals, withdrawing) and first steps (schedule activities, call sister).
sources: Beck-2021 § Ch. 21 Termination and Relapse Prevention

concepts.label: Booster sessions
concepts.definition: Scheduled sessions after the main course of therapy to review progress, consolidate skills and address early signs of relapse.
concepts.client_wording: Check-in sessions after therapy ends, to keep your progress on track.
concepts.example: Sessions at one, three and six months review the blueprint and a recent setback.
sources: Beck-2021 § Ch. 21 Termination and Relapse Prevention

concepts.label: Exposure and response prevention (ERP)
concepts.definition: Graded exposure to obsessional triggers while refraining from compulsions, neutralizing and reassurance seeking, so fear and urges reduce without rituals.
concepts.client_wording: Facing the things that set off obsessions, step by step, without doing the rituals.
concepts.example: The client touches a door handle and eats a snack without washing, sitting with the urge.

concepts.label: Video feedback (social anxiety)
alt_labels: self-focused attention and safety behaviors experiment
concepts.definition: Client predicts how they came across, then watches video of their social performance as an observer would, to correct a distorted self-image.
concepts.client_wording: Watching a video of yourself to compare how you felt you looked with how you actually came across.
concepts.example: Predicted "I'll look shaking and red" (80%); on video the client rates visible anxiety at 20%.

concepts.label: Cognitive processing therapy (CPT)
concepts.definition: Twelve-session trauma-focused therapy that identifies and challenges stuck points about the trauma and its implications using Socratic dialogue and structured worksheets.
concepts.client_wording: A structured therapy that helps you rethink unhelpful beliefs about the trauma and what it means.
concepts.example: The client's impact statement reveals "It was my fault for going out," the first stuck point targeted.

concepts.label: Stuck point challenging
concepts.definition: In CPT, identifying stuck points (beliefs that keep recovery stuck) and examining them with exploring questions, thinking patterns and alternative thoughts worksheets.
concepts.client_wording: Spotting beliefs about the trauma that keep you stuck, and examining them step by step.
concepts.example: "I should have stopped it" is examined against what the client knew and could do at the time.
sources: Resick-etal-2024 § Ch. 12 Session 7: Alternative Thoughts Worksheets

concepts.label: Prolonged exposure (PE)
concepts.definition: Trauma-focused protocol combining psychoeducation, breathing retraining, in vivo exposure to avoided safe cues, and repeated imaginal revisiting of the memory with processing.
concepts.client_wording: Gradually facing trauma memories and avoided safe situations so they lose their power.
concepts.example: The client recounts the assault in session each week and practices visiting avoided shops between sessions.

concepts.label: Cognitive therapy for PTSD (CT-PTSD)
concepts.definition: Modifies excessively negative appraisals, updates trauma memory hot spots, discriminates triggers (then versus now), and drops maintaining behaviors and cognitive strategies.
concepts.client_wording: A therapy that updates the trauma memory and helps you see that the danger is in the past.
concepts.example: The hot spot "I'm going to die" is updated with "I survived and the doctors said I recovered fully."

concepts.label: CBT for insomnia (CBT-I)
concepts.definition: Multicomponent insomnia treatment combining sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive therapy for sleep-related beliefs, sleep hygiene education and often relaxation.
concepts.client_wording: A structured program that resets your sleep habits and the worries that keep you awake.
concepts.example: Over six sessions the client keeps a sleep diary, restricts time in bed, and reworks fears about tiredness.

concepts.label: Sleep restriction
concepts.definition: Limiting time in bed to average actual sleep time from diaries, then adjusting it weekly by sleep efficiency, to strengthen sleep drive.
concepts.client_wording: Spending less time in bed for a while, so the sleep you get becomes deeper and steadier.
concepts.example: Diary shows 5.5 hours sleep in 9 hours in bed; the sleep window is set at 5.5 hours, then widened.

concepts.label: Stimulus control (insomnia)
concepts.definition: Re-associating bed with sleep: bed only for sleep and sex, leave bed when unable to sleep, fixed rise time, and no daytime napping.
concepts.client_wording: Retraining your body to link bed with sleep, not with lying awake.
concepts.example: After about 20 minutes awake, the client gets up, reads in another room, and returns when sleepy.

concepts.label: Sleep hygiene education
concepts.definition: Education about lifestyle and environmental factors affecting sleep, such as caffeine, alcohol, light and exercise; not recommended as a stand-alone insomnia treatment.
concepts.client_wording: Tips on habits and surroundings that help or harm sleep.
concepts.example: The client moves the last coffee to before noon and removes the phone from the bedroom.

concepts.label: Enhanced CBT for eating disorders (CBT-E)
concepts.definition: Fairburn's transdiagnostic, personalized eating disorder treatment in four stages targeting maintaining processes; usually 20 sessions, about 40 if underweight.
concepts.client_wording: A structured therapy that targets the habits and concerns keeping the eating problem going.
concepts.example: Stage one establishes self-monitoring, weekly weighing and regular eating before shape concern is addressed.
sources: Fairburn-2008 § Ch. 3 Enhanced Cognitive Behavior Therapy for Eating Disorders (CBT-E): An Overview

concepts.label: Collaborative weighing
concepts.definition: Therapist and client weigh the client once weekly in session, plotting and interpreting the trend, replacing frequent self-weighing or weight avoidance.
concepts.client_wording: Checking your weight together once a week and looking at the overall trend, not single numbers.
concepts.example: The client stops weighing daily; the weekly chart shows weight stable despite regular eating.

concepts.label: Regular eating
alt_labels: establishing a regular pattern of eating
concepts.definition: Establishing three planned meals and two or three planned snacks daily, without long gaps, to displace binge eating and dietary restriction.
concepts.client_wording: Eating at planned, regular times through the day, to break the diet and binge cycle.
concepts.example: Meals at 8, 1 and 6, snacks at 11, 4 and 9; binges fall from five to one a week.

concepts.label: Addressing shape concern and body checking
concepts.definition: Mapping overevaluation of shape and weight, developing other life domains, and reducing body checking, comparison and avoidance that maintain shape concern.
concepts.client_wording: Reducing how much your body shape and weight decide how you feel about yourself.
concepts.example: The client's self-evaluation pie is 70% shape and weight; they cut mirror checking and restart choir.
sources: Fairburn-2008 § Ch. 8 Shape Concern, Shape Checking, Feeling Fat and Mindsets

concepts.label: Behavioral parent training
concepts.definition: Teaching caregivers to use specific praise, positive attention, clear instructions, consistent consequences and reward systems to improve child behavior.
concepts.client_wording: Learning practical parenting skills that make good behavior more likely and conflict less likely.
concepts.example: Parents use a sticker chart for getting ready on time and praise each step within seconds.
sources: Kazdin-2005 § Key components of parent management training

concepts.label: Organization, planning and distractibility skills (adult ADHD)
concepts.definition: Adult ADHD modules: one calendar and task list, prioritizing, breaking tasks into steps, matching work chunks to attention span, and distractibility delay.
concepts.client_wording: Practical systems for planning, organizing and staying on task that suit how your attention works.
concepts.example: The client writes ideas on a distractibility pad and returns to them only after a 20-minute work block.

concepts.label: Safety planning
concepts.definition: Collaboratively writing a prioritized plan: warning signs, internal coping, social distraction, people to ask for help, professional and crisis contacts, and making the environment safer.
concepts.client_wording: A written step-by-step plan for keeping yourself safe if suicidal thoughts get strong.
concepts.example: The plan ends with calling or texting 988 and agreeing who will store medications safely for now.

concepts.label: Habit reversal training
concepts.definition: Awareness training, a competing response physically incompatible with the habit, and social support, used for tics and body-focused repetitive behaviors.
concepts.client_wording: Learning to notice a habit early and do something else with your hands instead.
concepts.example: When the urge to pull hair arises, the client clenches fists for one minute and records it.

concepts.label: Contingency management
concepts.definition: Providing tangible incentives, such as vouchers or prize draws, contingent on objectively verified target behaviors such as negative drug tests or attendance.
concepts.client_wording: Earning rewards for reaching specific goals, such as clean test results.
concepts.example: Each drug-negative urine test earns a voucher whose value rises with consecutive negative tests.

concepts.label: High-risk situation coping (relapse prevention)
concepts.definition: Identifying personal high-risk situations for substance use and rehearsing coping responses, including handling lapses to limit the abstinence violation effect.
concepts.client_wording: Planning how to handle the situations most likely to lead you back to using.
concepts.example: The client rehearses refusing a drink at a work party and plans what to do if a lapse happens.

concepts.label: Normalizing rationale (CBT for psychosis)
concepts.definition: Presenting unusual experiences as understandable and on a continuum with common experience, for example under stress or sleep loss, to reduce distress and stigma.
concepts.client_wording: Understanding that unusual experiences can happen to many people, especially under stress or without sleep.
concepts.example: "Many people hear voices after long sleep deprivation. Could stress and poor sleep be part of this?"

concepts.label: Early warning signs plan (bipolar relapse)
concepts.definition: Identifying the client's personal early signs of mania or depression and agreeing specific early action steps, often with family and prescriber.
concepts.client_wording: Spotting your own early signs that a mood episode may be starting, and agreeing what to do.
concepts.example: Signs: sleeping under five hours, starting many projects; actions: protect sleep and call the prescriber.

concepts.label: TRAP analysis (Trigger, Response, Avoidance Pattern)
concepts.definition: Mapping one recent episode as trigger, emotional response and avoidance pattern, including avoidant thoughts, to show how short-term relief maintains avoidance.
concepts.client_wording: Breaking down a time I avoided something: what set it off, how I felt, what I did.
concepts.example: Trigger: big project. Response: overwhelmed. Avoidance pattern: "I work best at the last minute," then sorts email instead.
sources: Knouse-Mitchell-2015 § Positively-valenced cognitive avoidance: a functional analysis; Figure 1 TRAP/TRAC model

concepts.label: TRAC plan (Trigger, Response, Alternative Coping)
concepts.definition: Planning an active coping step for the same trigger and response that usually lead to avoidance, then trying it and reviewing the result.
concepts.client_wording: Planning what I'll do instead next time the same trigger and feeling show up.
concepts.example: Same trigger and overwhelm; alternative coping: break the project into a 15-minute first step and start it.

concepts.label: Implementation intentions (if-then plans)
concepts.definition: Linking a specific cue to a planned action in an if-then statement, so the action starts when the cue occurs instead of relying on willpower.
concepts.client_wording: Deciding ahead: if this happens, then I will do that.
concepts.example: "When I notice the thought 'I'll just do it later,' I will work on the task for ten minutes."

concepts.label: Solution analysis (DBT)
concepts.definition: After a chain analysis, choosing a skill or change for each link, vulnerability and prompting event, plus ways to repair consequences.
concepts.client_wording: Working out what I could do differently at each step, and how to put things right.
concepts.example: Vulnerability: no sleep, so plan bedtime; link "I can't stand this": use a distress tolerance skill.
sources: Linehan-2025 § Chain analysis of problem behavior

concepts.label: Crisis response plan
concepts.definition: A brief, collaboratively written card listing personal warning signs, self-management steps, reasons for living, social supports and crisis contacts for suicidal crises.
concepts.client_wording: A pocket card we write together listing what I'll do and who I'll contact in a crisis.
concepts.example: Card: warning signs, take a walk, look at photos of my kids, text my brother, call or text 988.

concepts.label: Activity pacing (chronic pain)
concepts.definition: Breaking activities into planned, time- or quota-limited portions with breaks, regardless of pain level, to avoid overactivity and underactivity cycles.
concepts.client_wording: Doing activities in planned chunks with breaks, on good days and bad, instead of overdoing or stopping.
concepts.example: Gardens for 20 minutes, rests for 10, then 20 more, even though pain is low today.
sources: Nielson-etal-2013 § Abstract; provisional definition of activity pacing

concepts.label: Graded exposure to feared movements (chronic pain)
alt_labels: exposure in vivo for pain-related fear
concepts.definition: Exposure to a hierarchy of activities the client fears will cause pain or harm, to test those predictions and reduce pain-related fear.
concepts.client_wording: Gradually doing movements I've feared would hurt or damage me, to find out what really happens.
concepts.example: Bending to lift a light box after predicting "my back will give way."
sources: Vlaeyen-Linton-2000 § Implications for prevention and treatment

concepts.label: Grief exposure (revisiting the loss)
alt_labels: exposure to the reality of the loss
concepts.definition: Guided, repeated confrontation with memories of the death and avoided loss reminders, to integrate the loss and reduce avoidance in prolonged grief.
concepts.client_wording: Gently facing memories and reminders of the death I've been avoiding, so the loss can settle.
concepts.example: Retelling the day of the death in session, then visiting the grave for the first time.
